title: Flight 19: How Five Navy Bombers Vanished Off Florida in 1945
subject: avenger
description:
If you were in one of those cockpits, would you have turned west against orders? 👇

On the 5th of December 1945, five US Navy Avenger torpedo bombers took off from Fort Lauderdale on a routine training flight and never came back. A flying boat sent to look for them vanished the same night. This case file follows the radio calls, the Navy inquiry that first blamed the flight leader and then changed its verdict, the legend of the Bermuda Triangle, and why the wrecks have never been found.

Sources: Wikipedia, "Flight 19" and its references; Naval Air Advanced Training Command, Board of Investigation into 5 missing TBM airplanes and one PBM airplane (1945, via HyperWar); HISTORY (Evan Andrews, "The Mysterious Disappearance of Flight 19"; "This Day in History: December 5"); Skeptoid #417, "The Riddle of Flight 19" (Brian Dunning, 2014); The New York Times (Tim Golden, 5 June 1991).

scenes.text: Late on the afternoon of the 5th of December 1945, a Navy flight instructor named Robert Cox was flying near Fort Lauderdale when a strange conversation came over his radio.
A pilot was asking where they were. Another voice, calm at first, answered that he had no idea. Cox called in and asked what the trouble was.
The reply came from Lieutenant Charles Taylor, leading five bombers somewhere over the sea. Both of his compasses were out, he said, and he was trying to find Fort Lauderdale.
Taylor was sure he was over the Florida Keys, far to the south. He was wrong. And over the next three hours, that one mistake would decide everything.
Fourteen men were in those five planes. By midnight, thirteen more, sent out to find them, had also disappeared, and the Navy would never recover a single body.
The war had been over for three months, but Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale was still training crews on the Grumman Avenger, the heavy torpedo bomber that had fought across the Pacific.
That afternoon's exercise was called Navigation Problem Number One. Fly east to Hens and Chickens Shoals and drop practice bombs, then fly two more legs over the Bahamas and turn for home.
It was a triangle drawn over open water, meant to take about three hours. The student pilots, Marine and Navy officers, were close to finishing their training.
Their instructor was Taylor, a combat veteran of the Pacific who had recently transferred from Naval Air Station Miami. He did not know these waters the way he knew the Keys.
According to later accounts, he arrived late and asked if someone else could lead the flight. The request was refused.
One man stayed on the ground. Corporal Allan Kosnar had asked to be excused from the exercise, so one of the five planes took off with a crew of two instead of three.
At ten past two, the five Avengers lifted off and headed east over the Atlantic. Each one had a full load of fuel. The weather was good, but a front was moving in.
The bombing run went as planned. Around three o'clock, one pilot asked for permission to drop his last bomb, and got it. Somewhere after that, the flight lost its way.
The first words Cox overheard came from one of the students, Marine Captain Edward Powers. He said he did not know where they were, and that they must have got lost after the last turn.
Taylor saw islands below him and believed they were the Keys. If that were true, the mainland lay to the north and east. So he turned the flight north and east.

Investigators later concluded that the islands were almost certainly the Bahamas. The flight had been exactly where it was supposed to be, and every turn toward the northeast carried it further out to sea.

Ground stations asked Taylor to switch to the emergency frequency, where they could hear him better. According to the radio log, he refused. I cannot switch frequencies, he said. I must keep my planes intact.
Some of the students seemed to understand what was happening. One voice was recorded on the radio saying that if they could just fly west, they would get home. Head west, dammit.
Taylor changed course again and again. The sun went down, the sea below grew rougher, and the fuel kept falling.
At about twenty past six, a broken message came through. All planes close up tight. When the first plane drops below ten gallons, we all go down together.
Radio stations along the coast had worked out a rough position for the flight, far to the north of its planned route, east of central Florida. Rescue aircraft were sent toward it.
At 7:27 that evening, a Martin Mariner flying boat took off from Naval Air Station Banana River with a crew of thirteen. Three minutes later it sent a routine radio message.
The flying boat was never heard from again. Less than half an hour later, the crew of a passing tanker, the SS Gaines Mills, saw flames shooting up from the sea.
The ship searched the area and found a pool of oil and aviation fuel on the water. There were no survivors. A nearby escort carrier reported losing a radar contact at the same place.
The Mariner had a reputation. It carried tons of aviation fuel, its fuel lines were known to leak, and crews nicknamed these flying boats flying gas tanks. A single spark could have been enough.
By the next morning, hundreds of ships and aircraft were searching the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico and even the interior of Florida. They searched for days and found nothing.
Six aircraft and twenty-seven men were gone. The Navy now had to explain how it had lost them, with no wreckage, no bodies and only a radio log to work from.
A board of investigation met at Naval Air Station Jacksonville within days. Its report, hundreds of pages long, traced the flight turn by turn through the radio log.
The board concluded that Taylor had confused the Bahamas with the Keys, led his students out over the Atlantic, and refused the frequency that might have saved them.
The standard advice for a lost pilot at Fort Lauderdale was simple. Fly west, toward the sun, and you will hit Florida. Cox had told Taylor to put the sun on his port wing.
Taylor's family did not accept the verdict. His mother argued that the Navy was blaming her son for fourteen deaths without a single plane or body as evidence.
Under that pressure, the Navy changed the finding. The official cause of the loss of Flight 19 was rewritten to read causes or reasons unknown.
That phrase was meant to spare one man's reputation. In the decades that followed, it became the starting point for a legend.
In the 1960s, writer Vincent Gaddis put a name to the stretch of ocean between Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico. He called it the Bermuda Triangle, and Flight 19 became its founding case.

Books and films repeated the story, and it grew with each telling. In 1974, Charles Berlitz turned it into a bestseller. In 1977, Close Encounters of the Third Kind showed the lost planes found in a desert.

Some versions added radio lines that nobody in 1945 recorded. The researcher Lawrence Kusche went back to the original documents and reported that many of those dramatic messages had simply been invented.
The supernatural theories, magnetic forces, lost civilisations and visitors from space, rest on nothing in the Navy record. The compasses that failed belonged to one aircraft.
The ordinary theory is less exciting. Five planes, short of fuel, ditched at night in a rough winter sea. An Avenger weighed several tons and would have sunk quickly.
Against it, critics point out that not one life raft, oil patch or piece of debris from the Avengers was ever found. Supporters reply that the sea was huge, dark and violent.
In 1991, treasure hunters led by Graham Hawkes announced that they had found five Avengers on the seabed off Fort Lauderdale. For a few days, it looked like the case was closed.
The find did not hold up. The tail numbers did not match Flight 19. Those planes had been lost in separate training accidents, a reminder of how many young pilots this coast had already taken.
Between 1942 and 1945, according to the Fort Lauderdale base's own museum, ninety-five aviation personnel died in training accidents there. Flight 19 was the worst day, not the only one.
Most historians now accept the Navy's first account in its outline. A lost leader, a broken compass, bad weather and a stubborn turn away from the coast.
What remains open is the end. Nobody knows where the five Avengers came down, whether they stayed together, or whether anyone survived the landing on the water.
Late in the flight, Taylor finally agreed to head west. Holding two-seventy, he radioed. Then, doubting himself again, he wondered aloud whether they should turn back east.
The fourteen men of Flight 19 and the thirteen of the Mariner are remembered on memorials in Florida, including one at the old Fort Lauderdale air station, which is now a museum.

Robert Cox heard the first calls that afternoon and tried to talk them home. If Taylor had trusted the sun instead of the islands below him, those voices on the radio might have reached Fort Lauderdale.
